Similarly, if you could save five lives or two, you should save five. If you combine that with the surprising fact that most ordinary people can save lives routinely, and yet instead spend their money doing less effective stuff, then it seems obvious that people should start giving to effective global charities instead of the random charities that tickle their fancy. It’s intuitively pretty clear that saving lives matters more than giving to the charities you like.

Longtermism is another good example of this dynamic. The core idea of Longtermism is very basic. The one-sentence argument for Longtermism is: the future could have lots of people, meaning in-expectation almost everyone affected by our actions resides in the far future. Thus, given that people in the far future don’t matter much less than present people, we should aim to help them.

That sounds really obvious. If future people matter and almost everyone our actions affect is a future person, then we should look carefully into doing things that are good for future people. For every present person, there could be quadrillions of future people—intuitively, it seems like a single individual matters less than their quadrillion descendants. But in practice, almost no one pays much attention to how their actions affect the far future! Before the Longtermists, how many people spent any time thinking about how their actions would influence the very far future? Future thinking, before Longtermism, meant thinking about the next 200 years, not the next 2 billion.

It’s not that non-Longtermists explicitly think that people after 200 years suddenly stop mattering (if they don’t, then nearly all that matters is what will happen after 200 years). It’s that they simply don’t give the matter much thought. The idea that we should change our behavior in major ways based on how it will affect far future people is weird—but weird doesn’t mean wrong!

And sure, with Longtermism there are more complexities than with the core EA idea. To decide if Longtermism is right, you have to decide on slightly thorny questions like whether we can do anything to reliably better the far future. But it would be suspicious if, despite 99.9999% of the morally important impacts of our actions being on how they affect the future, there wasn’t any way that should affect our behavior.

Someone once joked that effective altruism is the paramilitary wing of analytic philosophy (note to people reading this named Emile Torres, please do not take this out of context and make it sound like EAs endorse violence). What he meant by this was that philosophers spend time thinking about ideas and uncover lots of non-obvious things to be done. Effective altruism is about putting those weird ideas into practice, when the ideas are neglected because people don’t think about them, not because there are serious objections to them.

Animal welfare is another good example. Even if you’re not some tree-hugging hippie animal lover, probably you have the intuition that animals being in pain is a bad thing. If someone was torturing dogs or pigs in their basement, that would be really bad! If you can prevent lots of animals from being in pain at very small cost, then you should do that. As a matter of fact, you can do this—a single dollar can prevent more than 10,000 shrimp from experiencing intense pain in death or can prevent chickens from spending around 10 years in a cage.

Thinking that this is a valuable thing to spend money on doesn’t require any eccentric views about animals. If there were 10 chickens who’d be trapped in a cage for a year unless you spent a dollar freeing them, that would seem like a good use of a dollar. If you value an hour of your life at $20, then this would be equivalent to spending 18 seconds freeing a chicken from a cage that would have otherwise trapped it for a year. If there were 10,000 shrimp who’d slowly suffocate unless you spent 1 dollar to stun them, that would seem like a good use of a dollar.

When you combine that commonsensical normative premise with the surprising fact about our world that a dollar really can prevent chickens from spending years in a cage, that implies we should change our behavior. But this radical behavioral change comes about because of a surprising fact about our world, not a counterintuitive moral premise. The moral premise that it’s good to spend a dollar so that sentient beings aren’t trapped in a cage for years is super obvious!

When EA activities look weird, that’s typically downstream of surprising facts about the world, rather than counterintuitive normative claims. It is a surprising fact about our world that you can help so many people and animals so cheaply. It’s similarly surprising that of all the welfare in human history, in expectation almost all of it will be in the distant future. I really like the way put this point when responding to a commenter who claimed it was counterintuitive to think we should fund humane pesticides:

Common intuition agrees: suffering is in itself bad to some extent, and hence worth reducing if you could do without undue cost or unintended side-effects. (Who would deny this?)

Common intuition agrees: scale matters. Two individuals suffering is twice as bad as just one, all else equal.

Crazy empirical premise: we cause (possibly unnecessary?) suffering to quadrillions of possibly-sentient beings.

Person who refuses to make logical inferences: “It’s *absurd* to think that the suffering of quadrillions of tiny beings could constitute a moral catastrophe! What are you, some kind of utilitarian?”

To prove EA rests on counterintuitive moral claims, you can’t just point to EA activities that sound weird. Weird doesn’t equal ethically counterintuitive. Norman Borlaug saved hundreds of millions of people by optimizing wheat production. That’s slightly odd behavior. But it wasn’t morally counterintuitive in any way—it was downstream of the surprising fact about our world that you can save hundreds of millions of people by optimizing wheat production. When the world is surprising, so too should our behavior be. I also like the way put it:

Many dudes come into EA because they’re into moneyball and then realize they can moneyball the good — but I was a little girl who liked to take care of babies, and I realized there were way too many babies who needed me, and I had to get smart about it if I wanted to save them all.

The core moral principle that one should do more good rather than less is intuitive. Often EAs recommend surprising behavior because in our world, the best ways to do good are slightly strange. But if you wouldn’t condemn Norman Borlaug for working on optimizing wheat production, you shouldn’t criticize EAs for helping shrimp or giving out vitamin A supplements. Sometimes doing good ends up being a bit weird.

item.title: Against Absolutist Deontology
item.content:encoded:
By Bentham's Bulldog

There are moderate deontologists and absolutist deontologists. Moderate deontologists say that you are sometimes permitted to perform seriously wrong actions if the benefits are great enough. Absolutist deontologists deny that. Moderate deontologists think you can kill an innocent person to save a trillion people, but not to save five people. Absolutist deontologists think you can never kill an innocent person (at least, in a prohibited way).

I think both views are wrong and I’ve given a number of reasons for this here. But absolutist deontology has significantly bigger problems than moderate deontology. The objections to it are, in my view, decisive. Unfortunately, closing the door on every option available to the absolutist deontologist is a lengthy endeavor—this piece will be quite long, around 5,000 words, but in most cases the long sections are responding to fairly in the weeds objections that you can easily skip. As Scott Alexander says, “the cost of thoroughness is length.”

Why should you read 5,000 words about absolutist deontology? To see how there really are proofs in philosophy, that it really is possible to establish non-obvious things by subtle argument. Philosophical progress is possible. To see, in addition, that no acts are absolutely impermissible—wrong to perform no matter how good their consequences are. The arguments in this piece, especially those in section 3, are some of the coolest arguments in all of philosophy!

1 Counterintuitive

Here’s a first problem with absolutist deontology: it is counterintuitive! It seems obvious that you should kill one person to prevent an infinite number of babies from being slowly tortured to death. If the only way to save the world was to kill one person, then you should kill that one person. This becomes clearer when you vividly imagine a world full of endless suffering, inflicted on babies, for all of eternity—all because of one omitted act that wouldn’t be very different from what people do daily. If the only way to save everyone on Earth from torture was to kill one person, then you should kill that one person.

My sense is this is the intuition that most people have, especially professional philosophers who have thought carefully about these things. Still, I don’t expect it to move the absolutist deontologist who probably does not find their view counterintuitive. Fortunately, we have other, better arguments.

2 Risk

The biggest problem for absolutist deontology: it struggles massively with risk. Absolutist deontologists think that it’s impermissible to kill an innocent person, no matter how large the benefits are. Even if shooting an innocent person would save the world, you shouldn’t do it.

But now ask: is it impermissible to risk killing someone? How much risk are you allowed to impose on someone to save the world? To see this, imagine a series of cases where you shoot someone with projectiles of progressively diminished lethality. At one end, the projectiles have a 99.9999% chance of killing them. At the other end, they have a 0.000000001% chance of killing them.

At what point does it become absolutely deontologically prohibited to fire the projectile to save many lives? There are three answers that the absolutist deontologist could give:

  1. Any risk is impermissible.

  2. Risks above some threshold (say, 40%) are impermissible. Perhaps the threshold is vague.

  3. Only certainty of death is impermissible.

Note: absolutist deontologists generally make fine distinctions between different kinds of actions that lead to death. They often think, for example, that you can kill innocent people in a just war or redirect a threat to save more lives. In all of the cases I am imagining, stipulate that the imposition of risk is not done in one of these ways that would make it permissible to take an action that leads to a death for a greater good.

It’s easy to see why 1 can’t be right. All actions impose some risk on people. If you shot a nerf gun at someone, there is some chance that it would trigger a fatal allergic reaction and kill them. Nonetheless, obviously it is permissible to shoot a nerf gun at someone to save the world. Some people maybe don’t find this obvious if they adopt the non-aggression principle—but even they will hold that it’s permissible to shoot a nerf gun vaguely in someone’s direction to save the world. But the problem arises: at what point does risking aggressing upon someone become impermissible? How high does the risk of the nerf gun hitting them have to be to be impermissible?

3 can’t be right either. No action ever imposes a 100% risk of death on a person—if you shoot someone ten times in the head, there is always some risk that a miracle will happen, or the gun will jam, or they survive by huge improbability, or that they have some weird genetic defect where their head is ridiculously hard. So this would mean that absolutist deontology never absolutely rules out any acts in the real world. Additionally, the problem I’ll raise for the next view involving sequences of acts also applies to this view.

The only remaining option is 2—that you can impose some risk of death on people, but it can’t pass some threshold. E.g. maybe you can impose risks up to 40% on someone, but never more than 40%. But this has a number of big problems.

First, it is objectionably arbitrary. Why 40% rather than 39.9% or 27%? Where did this threshold come from? You could say that it’s vague, but wherever the threshold vaguely kicks in will seem equally arbitrary (e.g. you may say that it’s absolutely impermissible to impose a substantial risk of death on someone no matter how great the benefit is, but why substantial rather than enormous or near-certain or some other vague predicate?)

It also doesn’t seem like the fundamental normative facts can be vague. It can’t be that there’s no fact of the matter about whether an act is absolutely prohibited. Either it’s absolutely prohibited, so that you’re morally not permitted to do it, or it’s not. It can’t be vague! It can’t be that there’s no fact of the matter about whether an action is categorically morally banned. Vagueness is (on my preferred view) a matter of the imprecision of language and/or mental representation, not of reality.

Second, and more concerningly, this has the counterintuitive implication that sometimes you are permitted to do A, permitted to do B, but not permitted to do A and B together as one act. Suppose that there are two actions which both impose a 30% risk of death on someone (both involve firing a projectile at some person which has a 30% chance of killing them). Each one saves a million people when performed. Assume that they each impose a risk of death on a different person. For instance, the first one might fire a projectile that leads to a 30% risk of death at John and the next would fire a projectile that leads to a 30% risk of death at Steve.

Each action would individually be permissible. But if you bundled them together as one act, then they’d be impermissible, because they’d have a 51% chance of killing someone. However, surely whether an action is wrong doesn’t depend on whether it’s counted as one act or two.

We can illustrate this in another way: imagine that there are two buttons which each impose a 30% chance of death on someone and save a million lives. Surely it wouldn’t matter whether you press the buttons as one act or as two. Yet if you press them as one act, with one hand motion, they’d exceed the risk threshold. And note: saying the threshold is vague doesn’t help at all, because a sequence of acts can still exceed a vague threshold, without any individual act surpassing the vague threshold.

I can see four ways out of this dilemma, each lousy.

2.1 Lifetime tally

First, you can think that you are never permitted, over the course of your life, to take actions which impose a risk of death on someone above some threshold (at least, in the way that’s morally culpable). So, for instance, over the course of your life you’d never be allowed to impose a more than 40% chance of death on anyone no matter how great the benefits are from doing so. That way, you could say that the first action is permissible but the second one is impermissible. The first act doesn’t exceed the threshold, while the second one does in combination with the first. If you take both acts together, then you’ll have exceeded the threshold.

On this picture, you have a running tally of “risk of death imposed on the innocent.” That tally can’t exceed some threshold, barring specific circumstances, like deaths in a just war or from the redirection of a threat, no matter how great the benefits of exceeding the threshold are. The threshold could also be vague.

The big problem with this view is that it makes the permissibility of acts bizarrely sensitive to other unrelated acts. Suppose that I’m deciding whether to fire a projectile at an innocent person which has a 40% chance of killing them but will save a billion lives. On this view, it matters whether a million years in the past, I imposed risk of death on some other innocent person for the greater good. But that is bizarre—why would such a thing be? Whether an act is wrong depends on the people it affects, not on whether it runs up some risk tally! Ironically, this seems, in a deep way, to violate the separateness of persons.

And what if you’re already above the permissibility threshold? Is every act that imposes any risk on someone impermissible? Nuts!

The view has another strange result. Suppose two people are deciding whether to perform an act that would have the exact same effects. It seems either both should do it or neither should. On this view, however, it might be that one person is permitted to do it and the other isn’t, so as the act raises one person above the risk threshold. That is bizarre—it shouldn’t be that Bob gets to fire the projectile that imposes a 40% risk of death, but Steve doesn’t because he did something similar a million years in the past. The view has even more problems—I’ll explain one more in a footnote—but I think this is sufficient to rule it out.1

2.2 Person-relative thresholds

The second way out: you can think that it’s impermissible to impose a risk above some threshold on any particular person. So, on this picture, you’re not allowed to perform an action if it imposes odds of death on someone in an impermissible way above some threshold, no matter how great the benefits are. For the actions A and B, because they impose risks on different people, they don’t contribute to the same threshold. Thus, A and B together would be impermissible only if either A or B was impermissible.

This view still has a number of problems.

First of all, the dilemma arises again in cases where the actions impose risks on the same person. Suppose that there are two projectiles that you can fire at John, each of which will have a 30% chance of killing him but each save a million lives. Suppose additionally that it’s impermissible to impose more than a 40% chance of killing John. On this view, each projectile would be individually permissible to fire, but firing them together is impermissible.

To get around this, you can hold that there’s a running tally of the risk you imposed on John. Because the second one would elevate John’s total odds of death as a result of you to above 40%, it’s impermissible. However, this is a very odd feature—why would whether I’m permitted to impose a 30% chance of death on John, who is very much alive, depend on whether a previous action imposed a risk on him, yet didn’t end up harming him? We can even imagine that the act imposed risk on John several billion years in the past—surely that shouldn’t be determinative of the permissibility of acts that impose a risk on John today.

Then, the second big problem for this proposal is that it fundamentally violates the spirit of absolutist deontology. Absolutist deontologists hold that it’s absolutely impermissible to do wicked acts, not just to do things which ensure any particular person is victim of a wicked act. To see this, imagine that you can throw a razor boomerang through a festival full of babies. It will kill a baby, but the risk of death imposed on any particular baby is low. Doing so will save a million lives. Absolutist deontologists should hold that doing so would be impermissible. And yet on this proposal, it would be permissible, so long as the risk imposed on any particular baby is low.

Note: any view that implies that throwing the boomerang through the baby festival is impermissible to save a trillion lives will have a problem with risk. Throwing a boomerang that imposes a tiny risk on a single baby to save a million lives is clearly permissible, if the risk is low enough—but if you multiply that, then you get the boomerang festival case. So any view that holds that throwing the boomerang through the festival will have problems with implying that taking sequences of permissible acts as one act is impermissible.

A third problem: the view requires bizarre individuation of people. Suppose I perform two acts, each of which have a 30% chance of killing someone (a different person each time). Each act saves a million people. Suppose the relevant risk threshold is 40%. Now, on the one hand, it might be thought that my sequence of acts is permissible. But now suppose that if my act harms one of the two people, it harms whoever is taller (so, for instance, each act might impose a 60% risk of death on the person if they’re the taller of the group). Additionally, let Tallee refer to whichever person is taller. Well, now my act has a 51% chance of harming Tallee.

Now, maybe you object that Tallee is not a person but instead just whoever has some property. What matters is whether there’s some specific person that you can point to who an action imposes a more than 40% risk of death upon. But this has more problems:

  1. This “pointing to” notion is vague. Does it require that you can see the person? What if you can only see them partially? What if, to borrow a memorable example from Caspar Hare, you can only see their fleshy ear? What if you additionally know that the taller person was called Tallee as a young child? Any time you know a person, what you really have learned is a number of properties about them—so knowing Tallee as the possessor of the property of being the taller of the two is only different from ordinary knowledge of people in degree, not of kind. And any threshold will be arbitrary.

  2. This makes actions counterintuitively sensitive to states of knowledge. Suppose that you will, in the above scenario, later learn which of the people is the taller one. Surely that shouldn’t change whether the act is permissible. But on this view, now that there’s some identifiable victim, it will have exceeded the risk threshold that you can impose on a known person. This has the strange result that there is moral reason to prevent yourself from learning anything about the potential victims of your acts, so that they don’t thereby become impermissible. It also violates Pareto.2

  3. This violates the spirit of absolutist deontology. Absolutist deontologists should hold it’s impermissible to kill, even if you don’t know anything about the people you’re killing. Imagine a blind person can shoot into an unknown crowd to save a million people. Absolutist deontologists should hold that that action would be wrong. But in this case, the blind person can’t identify any of the victims, so they don’t know who they’ll be harming.

Similarly, you get the same problem I highlighted in the previous footnote—where the proposal fails whether you use subjective or objective risk, plus the other problem in cases where you’ve already exceeded the probability threshold.

2.3 Knowledge

A third way out is to say that it’s impermissible to take acts that you know will kill someone. Knowledge, on this view, isn’t a matter of exceeding some quantitative threshold. Even if the odds I’ll win the lottery are lower than the odds that there’s no oat milk in my fridge, I might know that I have oat milk in my fridge without knowing that I won’t win the lottery. But this doesn’t help much.

First of all, there can be cases where you don’t know A, you don’t know B, but you know A or B. So, suppose that there are two acts. The first has a 50% chance of killing someone. The second one kills someone if the first one didn’t. You don’t know either kills someone, but you know they together kill someone. So problem with combining acts arises once more. This is also why the agglomeration problem arises for views that say there is only a categorical prohibition on imposing certain death on someone.

We can see this more vividly. Imagine that every day, you throw a razor boomerang with a 30% chance of killing someone, that saves a million lives. You don’t know, on any particular day, that you’ve killed someone. Nevertheless, you know that you will kill someone at some point over the course of your life.

Second, if this divorces knowledge from probability, then it delivers the result that actions that impose lower risks can be harder to justify than ones that impose higher risks. Suppose there is a 99% chance that there’s oat milk in my fridge (I just saw it) and a 99.99% chance that I won’t win the lottery. Suppose that nonetheless I know there’s oat milk in my fridge, but don’t know I won’t win the lottery. On this view, I am permitted to take an action that will kill someone if I don’t win the lottery to save many lives, but not permitted to take an action that will kill someone if I don’t have oat milk in my fridge to save many lives. But the first is strictly worse than the second, imposing a higher risk of death! If the view doesn’t divorce knowledge from probability, then it doesn’t help with the core challenge.

2.4 Individuation matters

A fourth way out is to bite the bullet and say that individuation of acts matters intrinsically. So, if acts A and B each impose a 30% risk of death on someone, they are impermissible if bundled as one act, while permissible if counted as two. Serious problems remain.

First, it’s not at all obvious that there are facts of the matter about whether acts count as one act or two. Is two button presses done in one continuous motion one act or is it two acts? It doesn’t seem like the moral law should make these fine-grained distinctions.

Second, even if there are facts about this sort of thing, it doesn’t seem like they’re morally relevant. It doesn’t seem to matter whether two acts are performed as one or done as two. If there are two buttons which each impose a risk of death on someone, it shouldn’t matter whether you press it in one continuous motion or two separate motions. It shouldn’t matter whether you fire two projectiles with one finger motion or with two.

Third, assigning some moral importance to whether two acts are counted as one produces weird Pareto violations. Suppose that it’s impermissible to impose risks of death on people above 40%. Now suppose that there are two ways to save a million people:

  1. Press one button that saves 500,000 of them while imposing a 30% risk of death on someone, and then press another button that saves 500,000 of them while imposing a 30% risk of death on someone.

  2. Press a single button that imposes a 40% risk of death on the person, and it saves all million people, plus an extra billion.

A view that cares about how acts are individuated—whether two are counted as one—counts the first as permissible but the second as impermissible. But this is bizarre—the second is better for many people, including the potential victim, and worse for no one.3

2.5 Conclusion

Note: any solution for the absolutist to the problem of risk will inevitably look like one of the proposals I gave. To see this, the paradox arises for the absolutist from the following contradictory affirmations (where A and B are risky acts that collectively but not individually exceed the risk threshold):

  1. It is permissible to take some action A which imposes a risk of death below the threshold on a person to save many lives.

  2. It is permissible to take another action B which imposes a risk of death below the threshold on a person to save many lives.

  3. Taking two permissible acts together as one act is permissible.

  4. Taken together as one act, actions A and B are above the threshold at which one can impose risks, and thus impermissible.

1-2 establish that A and B are each permissible, by 3, then, A&B together as one act would be permissible, but by 4 it’s not. Non-absolutists avoid this puzzle because they reject 4. If you reject 1, then you’ll get the result that it’s never okay to impose risks on people.4 If you reject 2, then you’ll think that B’s permissibility depends on whether A was done before. If you reject 3, then you think that how acts are divided up determines their permissibility. And if you reject 4, then you must either hold something like the view discussed in section 2.2 or reject absolutism.

3 Spectrum

Imagine the only way to save a million people is to fire a projectile at someone that has a one in a billion chance of killing them. This seems permissible—even required. You should shoot a nerf gun at someone to save the world, even though there’s some chance it will kill them.

But now imagine another action which has odds of two in a billion of killing them, which would save the million original people plus an extra million. Surely that is better. And a third action that would save a million extra people, while elevating risk of death to three in a billion (a slightly more dangerous projectile than a nerf gun) is even better. But if one continues down this process, one ends up with the result that shooting a gun at someone to save a very large population of people is permissible.

To avoid this, one must think there’s some threshold at which it stops being permissible to perform the act, even though the immediately prior point was permissible. But this would be bizarre! If you can impose a 19.9999% chance of death on someone by firing a slightly dangerous projectile, in order to save a billion people, then surely you can impose a 20% chance of death by firing a projectile that will save googolplex people. The second action is an improvement on the first—just a tiny bit of extra risk for a massive improvement.

And note: the spectrum doesn’t just arise with risk. Similar points arise with amount of time lost. It is permissible to shorten a person’s life by a single second to save a million people. But then surely it is permissible to shorten a person’s life by two seconds to save a billion people, and by three seconds to save a trillion, and so on. But at the end of this process, you’ve shortened their life by so many seconds that it’s brought about instant death in order to save a large number of people.

Now you might wonder: isn’t this just a Sorites argument (I’ll explain what this means in a footnote if you don’t know)?5 After all, aren’t we trying to identify the precise point where things shade from permissible to impermissible? Isn’t this like trying to identify when taking away a grain of sand makes something go from a heap to not a heap? No!

  1. The Sorites paradox arises from the vagaries of language. The fundamental normative facts aren’t about language. Impermissibility, as already described, doesn’t seem to be vague. While things can intuitively be vaguely a heap, or sort of a heap, things can’t be vaguely permissible.

  2. With the Sorites paradox, each time you take away a grain, it seems like the thing is getting less heap-like. Of the properties that make something a heap, it has fewer of those properties each time you take away a grain of sand. The puzzle concerns when it becoming less heap-like causes it to stop being a heap. This isn’t similar: at each step of the way, it seems the action is getting better! Each time it saves a million extra people. Formulated more precisely, the argument claims 1) the initial action which imposes slight risk of death to save a million people is permissible; and 2) each action in the sequence is better than the one before it, so the end action is permissible too. That’s not like the Sorites paradox, where the piles of sand are getting less heapy each time.

  3. If you go through all the solutions to the Sorites paradox—epistemicism, supervaluationism, nihilism—none of them provide a natural solution to this worry that doesn’t require biting bullets.

4 An intuition pump

I don’t consider this argument as forceful as the others, but it’s helpful for drawing out the core intuition:

  1. The fact that an action would save someone’s life gives you a reason to perform it.

  2. If 1. then you have infinitely strong reason to perform an act that would save infinite lives.

  3. The strength of your reason not to kill someone is only finite.

  4. If you have infinitely strong reasons to perform an act and finitely strong reasons not to perform it, you ought to perform it.

  5. Therefore, you should kill someone to save infinite lives.

You might try to reject 2 on grounds that there can be infinite sums of positive reasons that are only finitely weighty. For example, you have reason to extend a person’s life by a year, and other reason to extend a life by half a year, and by a quarter, and so on, but you don’t have infinitely strong reason to take this full infinite sequence of acts—that only adds two years collectively. But in that case, each action is less valuable than the rest, and the value of the acts asymptotically approach zero. Not so for saving lives.

The other premise to reject is 3. But a few things can be said in favor of 3:

  1. I think 3 is pretty intuitive. Naturally it seems that killing someone is very bad, but it doesn’t give you infinitely weighty reasons not to do it!

  2. If some action might be one you have infinitely strong reasons to avoid, then you should never risk it. But any time you step out of the house, there is some tiny chance that you will have some bizarre motivational shift and go on a killing spree. Notice that if there were a day during which if you killed anyone, this would cause infinite babies to be tortured, then it really would make sense to never interact with people on that day. On the absolutist picture, your reasons not to kill are similar.

  3. Suppose we’re looking at the strength of your reasons not to impose risk on someone. On this view, the graph will unnaturally spike to infinity.

5 Conclusion

Deontology writ large has a number of serious problems. I think it is very likely to be false. But moderate deontology, at least, has some hope. Absolutist deontology, in contrast, is, in my view, a complete non-starter. The objections—especially the second and third objections I raised—strike me as decisive. If you’re going to be a deontologist, be a moderate, enlightened centrist deontologist!

1

Another problem is construing what kind of risk the threshold is in terms of. Presumably it will either be subjective risk or objective risk. Subjective risk refers to how likely the decision-maker thought it was that an action would harm someone, while objective risk refers to how likely it actually is that the action would harm someone. Both have huge problems.

Suppose it’s subjective risk. Well, then that implies that if the decision-maker thought they were imposing a risk on someone in the deep past, that contributes to the threshold. But this is bizarre. If someone gave you a drug so that you reasonably thought turning on your lightswitch had a 30% chance of killing someone, that would not affect whether you should fire a projectile that risked someone’s death to save a million lives!

Suppose it’s objective risk. The problem is you don’t generally know objective risks. So this would imply that whether it’s permissible to risk harming someone depends on causally-isolated facts that you don’t know. But how can what you’re supposed to do, in light of your evidence, depend on things that aren’t part of your evidence? This also might imply, if the objective risks really are low, but you don’t know that, that you are permitted to take an action that for all you know has a 99.9999% chance of killing an innocent person.

What if it’s subjective risk that gets overridden if you learn objective risks? So, for instance, suppose you thought that an action had a 10% chance of killing someone but later learn that it really had a 40% chance of killing them, then you’d replace the amount contributing to the threshold from 10% to 40%? But on this view, you would treat wildly differently the contribution risk of the following two cases:

  1. An action leads to a coin being flipped, and if it comes up heads, someone dies.

  2. An action kills someone if the millionth digit of pi is even.

Because, assuming the millionth digit of pi isn’t even, the second one had a zero percent objective probability of killing someone, it would be treated differently in the calculus. It also isn’t clear that actions do have precise objective probabilities of killing people, as that depends on the reference class from which you’re counting objective probabilities. So, for instance, if you throw a sharp boomerang in someone’s direction and miss, is the relevant reference class total boomerang throws or missed boomerang throws?

2

Imagine that you currently, in the above scenario, know nothing about who the taller person is. However, in one hour, you will learn many things about them. Right now, you have the option to kill them painfully to save a million lives. In an hour, you’ll have the option to kill them painlessly to save a million lives. On this view, killing them in an hour will be impermissible (once you know who they are). That means you must kill them now, even though it would be strictly better for them if you killed them later. Now, there are many ways to try to wriggle out of this result, but Kacper Kowalczyk persuasively argues that none of them work.

3

Now, in theory, you could think that option 2 becomes permissible only if option 1 is present because it’s an upgrade over option 1. But this is an odd situation. Impermissible acts shouldn’t be improvements over permissible act sequences. Similarly, this runs afoul of the following principle: if there are two acts and one is individually impermissible, then if choosing between them, you should pick the permissible one. Additionally, this will still have the result that the first sequence considered on its own is permissible while the second is impermissible, even though the second seems obviously better than the first.

4

If it is okay to impose risks on people, then can cobble together a number of acts at the acceptable risk level until they exceed the threshold.

5

The Sorites paradox arises from the conflict between the following obvious-seeming principles:

  1. A single grain of sand is not a heap.

  2. A pile of a billion grains of sand is a heap.

  3. Taking away a single grain of sand never causes something to go from a heap to a non-heap.

item.title: Don't Shame People For Correcting Lies
item.content:encoded:
By Bentham's Bulldog

A while ago, I wrote a piece lamenting the existence of and correcting some particularly over-the-top lies about the Epstein files that were flooding short-form video social media. Among other things, a popular Instagram video creator claimed that the Epstein files depicted an infant being raped hundreds of times while their nine-year-old mother was being eaten alive.

Strangely, the mainstream media never reported on this scandal of the century! Similarly strangely, the way Sarah Olivia Rose thought to bring this scandal to light was by producing a nine second Instagram video that makes an audacious claim to pleasant background music but doesn’t provide any sources. Our standards really have dropped since the days of Woodward and Bernstein.

Occasionally, I would comment on the videos spreading the ridiculous lies, noting that the claims in them weren’t true. The replies, instead of providing sources for the outrageous claims in question, generally consisted of speculations as to my motives. Only someone really evil could be motivated to correct the claim that children are being eaten. Someone who does that might be a baby eater themselves—better watch out.

And my personal favorite:

Now, set aside the anti-semitism and the multi-pronged Talmudic confusion. Is it true that correcting false and scandalous claims—claims made up out of thin air—is “condoning pedophilia” or “apologizing for pedophilia?” Does it make a person one of “the most dangerous people on Earth.” No! Correcting lies is a good thing, even if the lies point in some politically convenient direction, lest the public sphere become a deranged maelstrom of falsity and nonsense.

These are particularly pathological examples of reacting negatively to people pointing out falsehoods and shooting the messenger (ironically, in this case, the messenger is bearing good news—that babies weren’t eaten). But the broader behavior is relatively common. People often are suspicious of the motives of those who correct false claims. For example, popular YouTuber Benn Jordan, with over a million YouTube subscribers, recently produced a number of videos about the alleged deleterious health effects of infrasound—sound beneath the frequency where it is detectable.

These videos were flashy and well-produced. They had only one big problem: nearly everything in them was false or misleading. You can read ’s excellent piece exposing Jordan’s videos, where he shows that every single source Jordan cites either says the opposite of what he claims or is pseudoscience.

In some cases, the audacity of the misrepresentation is truly beyond belief. Jordan supports the claim that “A meta-analysis suggests that [infrasound] can actually be pretty harmful to your health,” by flashing three papers that are not meta analyses and don’t suggest that infrasound can be harmful to health. One of these is a three-part report, with the conclusion Infrasound Does Not Explain Symptoms Related to Wind Turbines. If I was trying to support the claim that infrasound explained symptoms related to wind turbines, I do not think I would cite the claim “infrasound does not explain symptoms related to wind turbines.”

Similarly, a number of his “citations” involve flashing scary words from papers on screen, even when those papers explicitly attribute those symptoms to things that are not infrasound. This would be a bit like claiming that soup causes lung cancer by flashing words like “25% cancer risk increase” from a paper about smoking. Another source was an anecdote in a parapsychology journal investigating ghosts. Okey.

So what was Jordan’s response to Masley’s piece? Well, apart from his repeated hysterical denunciation on Bluesky, Jordan wrote a blog post responding to Masley. He claims Masley’s piece “seemed desperate and mean,” and complains about “being brigaded by someone deep in the Effective Altruism community. The author is, quite literally, paid by rotational-wealth NPO to write this very article among many others.”

Jordan’s piece contains a good deal of hand-wringing and histrionics, yet is substantively a barren void. He never addresses the many instances Masley points out of his sources saying the opposite of what he claims, preferring to bizarrely label EA a special-interest group and complain about the devious conspiracy by which receives money from Coefficient Giving, a charitable organization founded by Dustin Moskowitz who made his money through Facebook.

This is particularly baffling in light of the fact that Masley was writing about these issues before receiving any CG funding, Moskowitz has supported an AI pause, and Masley notes publicly that he’s funded by CG. The devious conspiracy that Jordan brought to light is that an organization dedicated to effective charitable giving also sometimes funds in broad daylight writers who promote effective charitable giving. He managed to uncover this conspiracy with an ingenious investigate journalism technique—going to Masley’s website and reading what it says (though ironically, not a technique he employed with regards to the studies he cited).

When Masley corrects Jordan’s lies, Jordan casts doubt on Masley’s character. The broader pattern is that if you correct falsehoods, you must have a good excuse for doing so. You must have some nefarious motive, beyond merely wanting to correct the record. This is deranged. Correcting lies is reason enough—you don’t need an independent, further reason.

I was subject to similar suspicions when I wrote an article about popular YouTuber ShoeOnHead’s lies about USAID. Shoe made a video lampooning USAID, seen by over a million people. Yet it had one notable if common defect, shared with Jordan’s video—much of what it said wasn’t true. Some of the false claims include:

  • USAID isn’t doing real aid because most of their money goes to contractors.

  • Huge amounts were spent teaching Sri Lankan journalists to use genderless language.

  • John Bolton was the head of USAID.

  • USAID’s initial function was purely to fight communism, not at all philanthropic.

  • USAID covered up a child sex abuse ring in Kenya.

  • USAID funded drug production in Afghanistan.

She also curiously omitted any discussion of the benefits of USAID in her calls to abolish it. This would be like glossing intervention in World War Two as “well, there was a lot of bombing,” without mentioning that we were fighting the Nazis who were trying to take over Europe and kill tens of millions of people. If you are going to seriously make the case for abolishing a program that has saved tens of millions of lives, rudimentary standards of honesty require that you mention some of its benefits, and don’t blast out easily checkable falsehoods to millions of people.

Many of Shoe’s supporters responded by claiming that I was bought off by USAID. As for Shoe’s own conduct, after lying repeatedly to over a million people, she doubled down.

While she admitted on Twitter that she was wrong to claim that Bolton was the head of USAID—a “fact” that she harped on repeatedly and at length throughout the video—she still, one year later, hasn’t bothered putting a correction underneath the video. Since she was informed that this was false, half a million extra people have seen the video (incidentally, half a million is a reasonable estimate of the number of people who died this year because of the policy Shoe carried water for). Yet Shoe didn’t bother to take twenty seconds so that half a million people wouldn’t be misinformed. And she has the audacity to lecture others about propaganda and disregard for truth.

This conduct from Shoe and Jordan is totally discrediting. A person who behaves this way cannot be taken seriously. If you can’t be bothered to correct lies after they’re pointed out, then you don’t value the truth. You’re not an honest actor. And if your response to your lies being exposed is to question the motives of the people doing the exposing—as a number of Shoe’s fans did, suggesting that I was bought off by USAID—you’ve begun to care more about your narrative than what’s true.

If It’s Worth Your Time To Lie, It’s Worth My Time To Correct It. We should be suspicious of the motives of the person who lied, not the person who corrected the lie. If you lie to carry water for the dismantling of an organization that prevents millions of children from dying, and don’t issue corrections when you learn your claims are false, then your motives are in significantly more jeopardy than those of the person correcting the lies. It casts much more doubt on someone’s character that they misinformed lots of people than that they corrected someone else who misinformed lots of people. As Scott says:

People don’t like nitpickers. “He literally did the WELL AKTUALLY!” If you say Joe Criminal committed ten murders and five rapes, and I object that it was actually only six murders and two rapes, then why am I “defending” Joe Criminal?

Because if it’s worth your time to lie, it’s worth my time to correct it.

If one side lies to make all of their arguments sound 5% stronger, then over long enough it adds up. Unless they want to be left behind, the other side has to make all of their arguments 5% stronger too. Then there’s a new baseline - why not 10%? Why not 20%? This mechanism might sound theoretical when I describe it this way, but go to any space where corrections are discouraged, and you will see exactly this.

I don’t have the words to describe the sheer depravity of this kind of disdain for the truth. It’s almost like something out of a C.S. Lewis story, designed to illustrate the corrosive effects of sin, to show the culmination of some nefarious plot by Screwtape to make his victim hate truth—to hate the light and love the darkness. You don’t need some extra reason to correct lies beyond the fact that they are lies, and the truth matters. Correcting popular falsehoods is a very good thing, and you don’t need some special excuse for why you did it.

So the next time you are tempted to claim that it sure is suspicious that this person felt the need to correct that particular lie—and call them a pedophile, a tech oligarch, or a CIA spy—STOP! Do not do this. If people cannot correct falsehoods without being accused of malfeasance, then falsehood will remain and rot and fester until the whole public discourse is nothing but fabricated, politically convenient, tabloid sensationalism. Truth dies where its defense is verboten.

item.title: Here's How You Can Make the AGI World Go Well!
item.content:encoded:
By Bentham's Bulldog

Two of my coworkers at Forethought— and —recently released a report called Concrete Projects in AGI Preparedness. The report describes concrete projects that could make a world of advanced AI go much better. I thought the report was worth signal-boosting in hopes that some of my readers will work on these amazingly impactful projects. My guess is that working on some of these has a non-trivial chance of making a genuinely major contribution to how well the future goes, where you could increase the expected value of the future by on the order of .1%, perhaps even more.

People in the past have had enormous impacts by working on important but neglected issues. Norman Borlaug saved hundreds of millions of lives by optimizing wheat production. Florence Nightingale saved millions by improving sanitation. Jonas Salk saved millions by inventing the polio vaccine. In a post-AGI world, we should expect there to be similarly—if not more—impactful projects. You can help make them happen.

If you’re interested in seriously working on these and want to get in touch, feel free to shoot me an email at untrappedzoid@gmail.com

1 Start an AI character evaluation org

The world is currently building very powerful AIs. Very few people are working on shaping the character of AIs. Very little research has been done on many of the important questions about AI character, like when AIs should refuse to cooperate with power grabs, whether AIs should have prosocial drives, and which prosocial attitudes are most effective for getting good character.

An organization could both empirically test these things and audit existing AI models for the quality of their character. That would give AI companies an incentive to shape AI character in a positive direction. As Will and Fin put it:

In particular, someone could set up an independent organisation to evaluate AIs based on traits like epistemic integrity, prosociality, and behaviour (including appropriate refusals) in very high-stakes cases. It could cross-reference the published model specs with observed behaviours in realistic, stress-testing conditions (e.g. multi-agent dynamics, long conversations with real people), to hold developers accountable. It could also give qualitative reviews of model specs.

In a world where advanced AI will perform most human labor and probably make most important decisions, positively nudging its character is unbelievably crucial. You can be directly involved in crafting the character of the superintelligent beings that will dictate the future.

2 Automated macrostrategy

Macrostrategy refers to big-picture strategic and philosophical reasoning about how the transition to advanced AI should go. For example, it might involve research into what kinds of regimes for digital rights there should be, or doing careful philosophical reasoning about how the intelligence explosion should go at a high level. Crucially, AI often lacks the ability to do this well. This is alarming; we are in for a dangerous world if AI is extremely competent in narrowly technical domains, but not good at the kind of big-picture thinking needed to navigate such a complex world.

For this reason, one high-impact opportunity is starting an organization working on speeding up AI macrostrategy. One could “create evaluations and benchmarks, collect human-generated training data, and build scaffolds to improve AI competence at big-picture strategic and philosophical reasoning.” More details in the post. I wouldn’t be surprised if working on this could speed up macrostrategy by months during a time when it is most critical.

3 AI security evaluations

There are reasons to think that AI could be used by malicious actors to concentrate power in a small number of hands. To prevent this, one could:

  • Run alignment audits on all AIs to detect sabotage.

  • Develop a “research sabotage” eval to test whether secretly loyal models could sabotage alignment audits.

  • Develop a model spec that prevents models from assisting users with illegitimate seizures of power (e.g., see “Preserving important societal structures” in Claude’s constitution), and one that’s suitable for government use of AI in the military.

  • Design and advocate for regulation, e.g. that AI companies have to demonstrate that any frontier AI does not have hidden goals.

4 Deals

There might come a point where AIs are powerful enough to attempt a takeover but not powerful enough to have any guarantee of carrying it out. However, later AIs might be able to successfully take over. In such a world, working out a deal with the early misaligned AI could be important. One could set up an organization that functions as a third-party broker to enforce deals.

(I’m probably a bit more skeptical about this).

5 AI for epistemics

Competent decision-making is an important part of having a good future. AI could be useful for designing tools to improve societal decision-making. You can work on developing tools so that collective decisions are made more rationally. There are a number of concrete ways this could be done that Forethought has explored, but to sum up some of the big ones:

  1. Community notes for everything: on Twitter, community notes beneath a post let you see if it’s misleading. One could roll out similar tools all across the internet, so that users could consistently see if they’re encountering misleading claims.

  2. Epistemic virtue evals: you could start a private organization that audits AI companies for their epistemic virtue—how responsive they are to evidence, how little bias they show, etc. This would incentivize developers to make epistemically virtuous AIs.

  3. Reliability tracking: this tool would allow you to comprehensively analyze the accuracy of the predictions of public figures, so that you can gather quantitative data on how much you should trust them.

The idea I’m most excited about is the better angel chief of staff idea, which Will and Fin explain in the following way:

Within the next year or two, we expect “AI chiefs of staff” to become widespread. These would be AI agents that manage your life, acting like a chief of staff, executive assistant, and personal and work advisor all in one. The design of these, and how they present information and nudge their users, could have major impacts on user behaviour. We could try to get ahead of this, building the best AI chief of staff, and designing it so that it helps users act in accordance with their more reflective and enlightened preferences.

I’m inclined to rank this a bit higher than Will and Fin—it strikes me as one of the most important ideas, perhaps just behind AI character.

6 AI for coordination

AI could be useful for fostering agreements. One could develop AI that acts as a trusted intermediary between key actors, verifying sensitive information without forcing it to be shared publicly. For example, you could imagine using this technology to verify that the terms of some arms control agreement were being followed without having to share sensitive information with an adversary. Alternatively, AI could be used to audit institutions and bring to light malfeasance without violating the privacy of key actors.

7 Space governance institute

Space is likely to be a big deal during the intelligence explosion. Actors who grab space resources quickly might have a big advantage. The primary determinant of how the future goes is how space resources are used, because nearly all the stuff in the universe is in space. Having an organization that works to craft space policy in an optimal direction could be important, but is currently very neglected.

8 Union of concerned ML scientists

Staff at machine learning companies often are morally motivated and hard to replace. For this reason, having a coalition of ML researchers who coordinate to try to make the intelligence explosion go well could be important. For instance, this group could recommend not working for company or government-led projects that could enable extreme concentration of power. They could also provide guidance on when to whistleblow.

9 Conclusion

It’s amazing how much low-hanging fruit there is to be picked. Many organizations that could be critical for things going well in a world of advanced AI simply don’t exist. By starting an organization to evaluate AI character, improve epistemics, or automate macrostrategy, you can meaningfully improve the transition to a world with advanced AI. Morally-motivated people working on problems like this have had some enormous successes— writes that at his first EAG:

I recall talking to a guy doing AI stuff at Google named Chris Olah; to Amanda Askell, then working on a philosophy PhD; to Buck Shlegeris, then a software engineer at PayPal.

…

I did not take this then-nonexistent technology remotely seriously enough, and the people I met who did take it seriously were able to do incredibly impactful work because of that. Chris Olah more or less founded the field of mechanistic interpretability (and coined the term!) and went on to cofound Anthropic. Amanda Askell is responsible for Claude’s personality and one of the most influential people in AI. Buck Shlegeris founded Redwood Research, perhaps the most interesting center of technical AI safety work outside of a major lab.

The track record of people changing the world by opting for maximum impact and carefully following the arguments where they lead is very good. The world is sleeping on the intelligence explosion—there’s so much left to do. You can be the one to do it.

item.title: Common Charity Assumptions Are Wrong
item.content:encoded:
By Bentham's Bulldog

Where did I go wrong? I lost a friend
Somewhere along in the bitterness
And I would have stayed up with you all night
Had I known how to save a life

—The Fray “How To Save A Life”

The core effective altruist moral claim is that one should make doing good as effectively as possible a key part of their life. This recommends that most of us change our behavior in two ways. First, we dedicate a bigger portion of our lives to doing good—take a high impact career if we can, give significant amounts of money to charity, and so on. Second, that when we’re doing good, we strive to be as effective as we can. The second of these requirements is often rejected (sometimes people say they accept it, but they rarely act on it). I don’t think it should be rejected.

When giving to charity, it is easy to myopically fixate on one’s own perspective. It is easy to only think about money being transferred to some organization or another, and not on what it will do. But the main effect of our charitable donations—the reason to donate—isn’t about money leaving our bank accounts, but the effects achieved.

Though the money leaving our bank account is most salient to us, it is not the most important thing. To regard it as what’s most important is to fall prey to a moral illusion, where we focus on what matters less, and ignore what matters more. As a magician may fool an audience by instructing them to look at what doesn’t matter, and ignore what does, we will be fooled if we don’t see what’s most important. It is the effect of the donation that matters most, and when we focus on that, the imperative towards cost effectiveness comes into view more sharply.

To see this, let’s imagine that you’re choosing between giving to the Make A Wish Foundation and the Malaria Consortium. The Make A Wish Foundation grants wishes to terminally ill children, so that they can have a bit of joy in their last days. The Malaria Consortium puts up anti-malarial bednets so that children do not die of malaria. Dying of malaria is very horrible— depicts a typical case in his moving article One Minute in Hell:

Aisha can’t breathe. Her palms are cold and pale. She presses her body against her mother, delirious and confused, seeking any comfort from the pain. She tries to cry but her voice is faint. She doesn’t understand what’s happening.

Like most severe malaria patients, Aisha is under five years old. A parasite is destroying her red blood cells faster than her body can replace them. Her nascent immune system was unprepared and was already weakened by malnourishment before she was infected by a mosquito bite.

Aisha was picking pink hibiscuses just two days ago, smiling proudly when she handed the bouquet to her mother. Malaria comes on fast. The disease is hard to detect and treat in small children because early symptoms mirror a dozen other common illnesses until it’s too late.

Aisha’s mother holds her and prays. Please, God. Please. Let it pass before the seizures. Give her any help, anything. She doesn’t deserve this.

It is much better to save someone’s life than to grant them a nice wish. Protecting Aisha is a much bigger deal than granting a wish. Take the money out of it. Imagine that, in your garage, you had a bunch of bednets. You could either put them up, preventing a bunch of people from getting malaria, and saving one of them from death, or you could instead grant a fun wish to a terminally ill child. You can only do one (perhaps the wish granted to the child would require using the bednets).

In this case, it seems completely clear that you should put up the bednets to save a life. If you’re choosing between saving a life and granting a wish, you should save a life. This is not to say that granting a wish to sick children isn’t important. If we lived in a fair and just world, every wish would be granted to every sick child. It is only to say that in a world filled with myriad horrors and profound injustice, one should prioritize dealing with the most severe evils that can be treated most easily. We are always in triage.

Think about the times you have been most ill—in your bed, with a high fever, retching and coughing. Malaria is worse, and it carries a serious risk of killing you. Every day, small children who are like your little brother or cousins die from this disease. Preventing that kind of evil cheaply is much more important than almost anything else our charitable dollars can do. If you think about what each donation achieves, it strikes me as clear that you should give to the Malaria Consortium instead of to ineffective charities.

Along these lines, consider the famous drowning child argument. Imagine you’re on your way to donate an expensive watch to a charity—which would be sold to raise $5,000—when you see a child drowning. Crucially, the watch clasp is very complicated, so you won’t be able to take it off in time. If you wade into the pond, the watch will be ruined. Nonetheless, it seems you ought to wade into the pond, because saving the child is more important than making a donation to the charity. But when you give to minimally effective charities, you are putting inefficient charity over saving someone’s life.

Now, there are a few differences between the cases, but none of them seem to have sufficient moral importance to make it permissible to give to the less effective charities.

First, effective charities are generally preventative. They prevent people from getting sick, rather than treat them after they get sick. But surely preventing is not worse than treating. It is commonly assumed, in fact, that it is better. What matters is saving a life, not how it’s done.

Second, they’re generally less direct. When you give to an effective charity, there are a few more steps in the causal chain before you save the person’s life. But this doesn’t seem morally relevant either. Imagine if, in the earlier case, you had to sell the watch to buy a rope to pull the child out of the pond. Though the causal chain would be slightly tangled, you’d still be obligated to do that. What matters is saving a life, not the complexity of the causal chain.

Third, the children saved by charity are further away. But your obligation to save a life doesn’t go away because the person saved is further away. To see this, imagine that instead of wading into the pond saving a nearby child, it allowed you to push a button at the bottom of the pond that saved a far away child. Still, in such a case, you’re obligated to wade into the pond to push the button. Again, what matters is saving a life, not how far away the life saved is.

If you want to hear more analysis of the drowning child argument, see here. It’s a useful intuition pump, because it makes clear what really is at stake. This isn’t an intellectual game, nor is charitable expenditure some exotic personal art project, where its sole purpose is self-expression. Where you choose to donate affects how many children die. That is far more important than whether the charity you give to resonates with you emotionally.

It’s also helpful, when deciding how people donate, to consider how you would want to donate if you cared deeply about all the people affected. Imagine, in the case where you are choosing between giving to the Against Malaria Foundation and the Make A Wish Foundation, that the people being helped were your brother and sister. The Make A Wish Foundation would grant a day of enjoyment to your brother, while the Against Malaria Foundation would save the life of your sister.

Wouldn’t it seem obvious that if someone was choosing just one to donate to, they should give to the Against Malaria Foundation? That they should prioritize saving the life of one of your siblings over granting a single day of enjoyment to the other. And shouldn’t we, in our treatment of strangers, at least try to mimic the behavior we’d carry out if we cared deeply about them?

We go wrong in thinking of charity as some homogenous bucket, where giving is a generic nice thing. But not all charities are the same. When people’s lives are on the line, we have a duty to help people as much as we can, rather than help them in the way we like best. A firefighter has a duty to save as many people from a burning building as he can, not to pick the route that he likes best. A doctor treating many sick patients has a duty to do triage, and prioritize the patients that are easiest to help. It would be obviously immoral for a doctor to instead just treat the diseases that they feel the best about helping. Though we do not typically realize this, we are like the doctors and firefighters, in that we are able to save lives routinely.

You might wonder: what about the non-global-health charities? Some EA charities prioritize mitigating catastrophic risks. Others prioritize animal welfare. If, as I say, we are always in triage, surely those can’t come before helping people? If you can’t prioritize the Make A Wish Foundation over saving someone’s life, why can you prioritize reducing existential risks over saving a person’s life?

In order to make the case for giving to some other charity over global health charities, you really do need to be convinced that it does more good than saving lives. But I think it’s plausible that there are charities like that. My guess is that it is significantly better to give money to Longtermist charities than global health charities.

Similarly, I really do think that careers spent mitigating existential threats are higher impact than careers spent working on global health. In these careers, you can be one of a few dozen or hundred people working on some of the world’s biggest problems. Despite there being only a few hundred alignment researchers, experts consistently think that the odds of misaligned AI ending humanity are a few percent—I’m seen as a crazy moderate for putting the odds only at around 2%. And other risks are even bigger and more neglected.

There are both practical and philosophical reasons to give to Longtermist organizations—ones reducing existential threats, safeguarding the future, and preventing cataclysmic jeopardizing of most future value.

The practical reason: there are threats to the world that have a non-trivial chance of ending it. Almost no one is working to address them. My guess is that there are Longtermist projects which individuals can carry out that have non-trivial effects on how the future goes. Some of these projects plausibly can increase the expected value of the future by on the order of .1%. Lowering the risk of an engineered pandemic that kills billions of people can be more valuable than saving an individual person’s life. Improving AI character could make things better for everyone on Earth, once AI takes over increasingly large shares of the world.

A .1% chance of an engineered pandemic that kills a billion people imposes a 1/1,000 risk of death on a billion people. Yet a 1/1,000 risk of death imposed on a billion people is as bad as the death of a million people (for that is how many people are expected to die, and this threat to life doesn’t become less bad because the people’s deaths are correlated with each other). So then working to lower the risks of catastrophes can be better than working on global health.

When evaluating the expected badness of a risk of some potential horrendous outcome, you ought to multiply the odds of the horrendous outcome by how bad it would be. When evaluating how much of a difference you can make, multiply its expected badness by your chance of making a difference. So a 1% chance of preventing an engineered pandemic that would have a 1/1,000 chance of killing a billion people is as good as saving 10,000 people. For this reason, I’d recommend a career in pandemic preparedness over one in global health.

There is also a moral argument for working on Longtermist causes. Almost everyone affected by our actions is in the future. The future could contain an incomprehensibly greater number of people than the present. When people try to model how many future people there could be, they end up with numbers like 10^58, and sometimes orders of magnitude greater.

The gulf between the number of people on earth today and the number of future people there could be is far greater than the gulf between the first human on earth and all their descendants. As it would have mattered a lot for the first human not to screw up life for their more than 100 billion descendants, it matters a lot that we not screw things up for our incomprehensibly greater number of descendants. It is amazingly important that the future contains joy and bliss and love in quantities too abundant to fathom. As Nick Bostrom says of future lives:

If we represent all the happiness experienced during one entire such life with a single teardrop of joy, then the happiness of these souls could fill and refill the Earth’s oceans every second, and keep doing so for a hundred billion billion millennia. It is really important that we make sure these are truly tears of joy.

For more on why nearly all that matters in what we do is how our actions affect the far future, see here, and for more on why ensuring well-off people to come into existence is important, see here. Though even if you didn’t think ensuring the future had a lot of people was important, still the best actions would mitigate the odds of really bad futures. If future people matter, and we can affect them, they are so numerous that almost all of what matters is how our actions affect the distant future.

So when I bring up that some charities save lives, I am not suggesting that no actions can ever be better than saving lives. I am saying that in order to justify some act of charity that doesn’t save lives, there should be a plausible case that it’s better than saving lives. We live in a world of such profound malleability—where nightmarish evil or boundless good may be brought about, depending on how we act—that some actions we can take really are better than saving lives. It was better for Norman Borlaug to optimize wheat production and save a billion lives than to become a doctor; some of our opportunities may be similar.

When you choose which charity you give to, you are choosing between different outcomes—different things in the world to bring about. One of the outcomes you can bring about is that a child’s death is averted. In order to justify bringing about some other outcome instead, that other outcome must be hugely important. Now, I think there are some outcomes like that—like lowering the risk of certain really terrible outcomes—but not any old outcome you feel like bringing about will do.

Similarly, I don’t want to claim that you have to make a binary choice between effective giving and giving where you want. Give 10 bucks to your local soup kitchen if you want. What you have a duty to do is to make effective charitable giving an important part of your life—to have most of your giving be as effective as you can make it.

If you often try to save drowning children, but then occasionally engage in less effective charitable endeavors that mean more to you, fine. Just as it’s okay—suboptimal but not morally prohibited—to spend money on yourself, it’s fine to spend money on charities that are not maximally effective. It would be odd if you were permitted to spend money on a meal out, but not give that money to an ineffective charity. But you should make sure that a big part of your life is doing good as effectively as you can. Extra ineffective charitable giving on top of this can be thought of as akin to a personal indulgence, rather than something that discharges that central obligation.

That is the core upside of thinking in terms of effects rather than the money donated itself. When you vividly hold in your mind that when you give to charity, you are choosing between different things to bring about, and one of them averts the death of a child, then it becomes clear that laissez-faire moral views according to which one can donate however much they want wherever they want are untenable. We have been afforded extraordinary opportunities to make the world a better place—we ought to take them.

item.title: Fine-Tuning Clearly Needs Explanation
item.description: Almost any other view is more plausible than thinking fine-tuning is brute
item.content:encoded:
By Bentham's Bulldog

Certain parameters in physics fall in a very narrow range needed for the formation of life. If they didn’t fall in this range, either the universe would have just been floating clouds of hydrogen gas, or all particles would immediately fly apart, or the universe would immediately collapse. The physics behind this claim is largely uncontroversial. As theoretical physicist Aron Wall, who provides very measured and balanced takes on these sorts of things, put it:

It is not controversial among physicists that these “anthropic coincidences” exist. Even atheistic physicists who work in the relevant areas mostly acknowledge it is true. The question is what is the explanation for this phenomenon?

Of the values the cosmological constant could have taken on, only about 1/10^120 of them would have made any life possible. That’s about the odds of throwing an atom-sized dart across Earth and hitting the same atom three times in a row, then winning a one in a million lottery twice in a row. You shouldn’t think such an astonishing coincidence happened merely by chance. That theism can explain such a puzzling phenomenon is a good argument for believing in God. Probably you have a bunch of objections at this point—I’ve tried to address them comprehensively here.

Fortunately for atheists, there are much better options available than attributing this to chance. You can explain fine-tuning with a multiverse. I think this explanation has some problems, and fine-tuning remains strong evidence for theism, but it’s much, much, much better than eating the hit on a 1/10^120 coincidence. You should never do that if there’s an alternative explanation that isn’t comparatively implausible.

But some people think fine-tuning doesn’t need an explanation. These people think that it doesn’t make any sense to talk about the odds of the parameters having some value. It isn’t as if there was some random process that selected the parameters, making each value equally likely. So we can’t call such a thing probable or improbable.

I think this position is about as wrong as anything could be.

Let’s first be clear on the kind of improbability we’re talking about. It’s called antecedent epistemic improbability. This is how unlikely you would have found some event before you knew it was the case. Crucially, some proposition can be epistemically improbable even if you now know it’s likely and it couldn’t have been any other way consistent with the laws of physics.

If tomorrow we discovered that there were 10^100 particles in the known universe, we would subsequently know that with high confidence. Nonetheless, it would be highly antecedently epistemically improbable in that before knowing it was the case, you would have had a low credence in it being true. Something can have been antecedently improbable even if you now know that it’s true: if someone gets an extraordinary string of luck in poker, you now know that they got lucky, so the probability that they got so lucky is 100%. But still, you can reasonably say that something improbable happened, in the sense that you would have reasonably assigned a low probability to it happening before it happened.

And crucially, for something to be epistemically improbable, there doesn’t have to be some random selection process that leads to it a low percentage of the time. A lot of the evidence for continental drift comes from the fact that the fossil records of continents started diverging at discrete points in the past, and the continental shelfs fit together like a jigsaw puzzle. We can reasonably say that such a pattern is unlikely unless continental drift happened, even though we don’t have any repeated experiments of such things.

Similarly, one of the major lines of evidence for atomic theory was that there were many different ways of calculating Avogadro’s number that all converged on the right answer out to many decimal points. It is reasonable to say that such a thing would be improbable if atomic theory was false, even though there would be no random selection process for determining the values that they would take on. Rather, it would be epistemically improbable that such ways of calculating the values would return convergent results.

Let’s look at some cases of this kind of reasoning closer to the fine-tuning case.

Imagine that the initial conditions of the universe spelled out “made by God, with love,” in every human language. That would be very surprising. It would be surprising even though we’d then know that it was true, and it would be physically necessary. The reason it would be surprising is that out of all the shapes the initial conditions could take on, it’s unlikely they’d take on that specific one. In contrast, a theory on which there was some designer would render it less unlikely that the initial conditions would take on such a shape.

I think of fine-tuning as working similarly to this case. We notice some surprising pattern in the laws and constants, we see that the pattern is both highly specific and very valuable, and so we attribute it to design absent a better explanation.
