This is a very normal inference: if you saw a space ship appear in the sky and begin shooting lasers, you should think it was caused by an agent, even though it could, in principle, be produced by a random physical process. We invoke design as an explanation when something is very improbable by chance but the kind of thing that an agent might get up to.

Here’s one case that seems especially close to fine-tuning and shows that you shouldn’t just declare fine-tuning brute.

Imagine that there were two physical theories. One of them entails that the value of some parameter will be one of a hundred possible 120-digit numbers. The other places no constraints on the value of that parameter—it could be anything. Now imagine that we find that the parameter takes on one of the values that the first theory predicts it must. Surely that is evidence for the first theory!

This is very similar to fine-tuning.

Theism makes predictions about what the constants will be. It doesn’t make certain that the constants would be finely-tuned, but it at least makes a finely-tuned constant not astronomically improbable. So theism is like a theory that narrows down a physical parameter to 100 options (or 1,000, or 10,000 or whatever). Single universe atheism, imposing no constraints on the value of the constants, is like the theory that leaves the constant unconstrained. If the constant is one of the 100 options, that obviously confirms the first theory over the second!

I see two options available for the in-principle opponent of fine-tuning: biting the bullet and arguing that the cases are non-parallel.

How might they argue that they’re non-parallel? One way is to suggest that theism doesn’t place any constraints on the value of the constants. But this surely isn’t right. If there was a God, the odds of the cosmological constant falling in the range that gives rise to life and complexity without needing direct divine intervention surely aren’t astronomically low. Surely the odds of such a thing happening aren’t one in googol?

If you knew God existed, and we had the physical laws we do, you would not be as shocked to find the cosmological constant fine-tuned as to hit the same atom with a dart thrown randomly across Earth three times in a row, then win the lottery twice. Perhaps you think you would be that surprised. Well, there are lots of smart people who don’t think it’s that surprising. When smart people disagree with you, and they’re not kooks, you should not think the odds that they’re right are on the order of the odds of hitting the same atom thrown randomly across the known universe three times in a row.

Second, you might bite the bullet and simply deny that this would be evidence. This is very hard to seriously maintain when one thinks vividly about the case.

Imagine the partisans of each theory entering the room, neither having been informed of the value of the parameter. The first one predicts that it will be one of a hundred specific 120-digit numbers—the other has no guesses. You read off the digits. After digit five, the partisan of the first theory has narrowed it down to just one possible remaining number, and goes on to correctly predict the next 115 digits. The partisan of the other theory has no expectations, being continually surprised by each passing digit.

Surely, in such a world, you should update in favor of the first theory! That is because their theory renders some otherwise extremely unlikely phenomena insanely unlikely, while the other theory does not. And, of course, whether this is evidence doesn’t depend on whether you actually bother bringing the partisans of the theory into the room, and have them guess the constants values.

Now, again, I am not saying that you have to give up atheism in light of fine-tuning. I am merely claiming that if you say fine-tuning has no explanation, that the constants taking on such an astronomically improbable value is purely a matter of chance, and there’s nothing more to be said about it, then something has gone badly wrong in your reasoning. You will have to eat the hit on a coincidence on the order of hitting the same atom thrown across Earth three times in a row and then winning the lottery twice. Most alarmingly, you have abandoned Bayesianism!

When analyzing fine-tuning, I often feel like people go into debate mode and become too unwilling to concede ground. They often start endorsing extremely speculative proposals in physics that physicists don’t take seriously to avoid giving ground. It is perfectly fine to admit that some fact is a bit surprising and poses some evidence against your worldview. I admit that about the fact that the world is filled with evil is evidence against theism.

I hope I have built up some credibility when analyzing theistic arguments. I do not think that all of them are good. In fact, of William Lane Craig’s common arguments for theism, fine-tuning is the only one I think has much force, and most I regard as dismal failures. But fine-tuning is really puzzling, and if you don’t feel that something weird’s going on, then I think you’re fundamentally missing the force of the challenge.

Here’s what I would say about fine-tuning if I was an atheist. First of all, atheists have a pretty good explanation of fine-tuning in the form of a multiverse. Second, theism doesn’t explain it as well as people naively think, because God could create life in myriad ways. He could create direct, joyous, disembodied minds, or make any arrangements of matter conscious, or create directly by miracle. So when you combine these factors, fine-tuning is only moderate evidence.

Now, to be clear, I don’t agree with this line. I both think fine-tuning isn’t that unlikely given theism and a multiverse given atheism is very unlikely. But it doesn’t strike me as crazy, and it doesn’t require warping one’s assessment of how probability works. I’m worried that people, in an attempt to resist the fine-tuning argument, often endorse extremely implausible things, and this makes their worldview make a lot less sense.

So go in for a multiverse, or deeper physics, or some expansive naturalistic alternative like axiarchism. Just don’t say fine-tuning is brute! That explanation is wholly untenable, and trying to maintain its tenability risks infecting the rest of your probabilistic reasoning and distorting the plausibility of your worldview.

item.title: Every View of Population Ethics Agrees: Proliferate Happy Lives!
item.description: So then let's do it if every view says it's overwhelmingly important!
item.content:encoded:
By Bentham's Bulldog

1 Introduction

Lots of utilitarians think that ensuring the world has happy future people in enormous numbers is overwhelmingly important. Non-utilitarians often claim this judgment is weird and counterintuitive. But really, the judgment isn’t something tied to utilitarianism. It follows so long as you think it’s good for happy future people to be created. As I’ll argue, every view of population ethics on the market implies that it’s good to fill the universe with happy people, even ones where it doesn’t seem like they imply that.

Before we get into the nitty gritty, I want to make clear that it strikes me as pretty intuitive that creating lots of happy people is good. It’s good to live a great life. I’m happy that I exist, and get to experience all the awesome things—beauty, love, friendship, happiness, writing 15 billion words about why deontology is false—that accompanies a complete life. It is good that Earth is filled with happy people, spanning continents, and it would be a lot worse if there were only like 100 happy people on some island. Theron Pummer (before defecting to the dark side and adopting the person-affecting view) put it nicely:

suppose I could push a button that would create billions of happy people living on several large and lush Eden-like planets. These people would in turn produce further generations of happy people, who would do likewise, and so on for the foreseeable future. Pushing the button would cost me nothing and do no harm or wrong. Would it be wrong of me not to push the button, in this case? Yes, I believe it would.

A survey by David Althaus, Andreas Mogensen, Geoffrey Goodwin, and Lucius Caviola found that most people’s intuitions on this are similar. They think it’s good to create happy people.

If creating happy people matters, this has very significant practical implications. It means that we should use the resources in space to create well-off conscious beings in enormous numbers. Given just how great the value of such an act might be, ensuring that this gets done is the most important thing.

Note: there’s disagreement on exactly what makes a person well-off. Some say that it’s being happy, others that it’s having your desires fulfilled, and still others say that there’s a list of goods that contribute positively to welfare. So not everyone will agree on precisely which well-off future beings should be proliferated. But everyone should agree that proliferating them is very good. So long as we fill space with minds that score highly on every view of well-being, that would be very good.

Let’s see what every view of well-being has to say.

2 The easy cases

Perhaps the most popular view of population ethics is the total view. This says that the welfarist value of a world equals its total welfare. So if you want to figure out which of two worlds are better with respect to welfare, just add up how much total welfare is in each world. Whichever is greater is better. I say with respect to welfare, because there might be other things in a world that matter, like whether people are getting what they deserve and how much nature there is. But that’s orthogonal to theories of population ethics.

Lots of people reject the total view because it implies that for every great world, there’s another, better world full of just barely happy people. Others (myself included) think this result isn’t so bad. But in any case, it’s very easy to see why the total view implies that creating happy people is great. It raises total welfare.

Another popular view is the critical value theory. This says that adding someone to the world is good only if their welfare passes a particular threshold. If it doesn’t, then either it’s bad or neither good nor bad. But on this theory, of course, proliferating well-off people above the threshold is good.

3 Person-affecting views

What about the person-affecting view? This says that it isn’t good to create happy people. The sloganized form of the PAV: make people happy, not happy people! However, there is a subtle way that the PAV implies that we should create happy people in enormous numbers, slogan be damned.

To see this, first imagine a person undergoes a hemispherectomy, meaning that one of their hemispheres is destroyed. Surely, in this case, it is better for them to survive the hemispherectomy than not to survive it. Having one successor is better than having none. So from this we conclude: it’s good for one of your hemispheres to be saved, even if the other is destroyed.

But now imagine that instead of the other hemisphere being destroyed, it is simply transferred into another skull. Let’s call the person that gets the right hemisphere “righty” and the other one “lefty,” (the first one supports the second amendment and lower taxes, while the second one has blue hair). Then ask: is it important that the transplant of lefty is successful?

It seems that the answer is yes. After all, we’ve already seen that it would be important that lefty survives if their right hemisphere was to be destroyed. Surely it shouldn’t matter whether instead of being destroyed, their left hemisphere is transplanted somewhere else—perhaps elsewhere in the galaxy. So we have the following argument:

  1. It is good for the right hemisphere to go on if the left is to be destroyed.

  2. It is as good for the right hemisphere to go on if the left is to be implanted as if the left is to be destroyed.

  3. Therefore, it is good for the right hemisphere to go on if the left is transplanted.

  4. It is similarly good for the left hemisphere to go on if the right is transplanted.

  5. Thus, it is better to have two successors—lefty and righty—than just one.

How should we explain this? Parfit’s proposal is that what matters is the R-relation. You’re R-related to someone if they are psychologically continuous and connected with you. You are R-related to your future self because your psychological state at each moment is connected to the ones before.

If R-relation is what matters, then it is very good to fill the universe with happy digital minds. So long as those happy digital minds are psychological successors of current people—having, in their first moment, reasonably overlapping mental states—then filling the universe with them would be good. Just as it’s better to be succeeded by lefty and righty, it’s better to be succeeded by two psychological successors than just one.

What if R-relation isn’t what matters? Perhaps one could think that what matters is identity. But identity must be transitive. I cannot be identical to both lefty and righty, so this view inevitably leads to identity being extrinsic. Whether I survive one of my hemispheres being transplanted would depend on what is done to the other hemisphere, perhaps galaxies away. (You can get around this by believing in souls, but I don’t know of any proponents of the person-affecting view who believe in souls).

So far, we’ve seen that:

  1. Identity can’t be what matters without being extrinsic. But it isn’t extrinsic.

  2. It is better to have two successors than one.

The most natural explanation of this is that the R-relation is what matters, and it is better to be R-related to two people than one. If what matters cannot be identity of any kind, or otherwise it would be extrinsic, then the only remaining potentially mattering relation is the R-relation. But then having many psychological successors is better than having none.

What about averageism, which says that the welfarist value of a population is a function of its average welfare? Now, averageism is very implausible and rejected basically by everyone, because it implies that it would be great to fill the world with horrifically miserable people, so long as they were slightly less miserable than other very miserable people. But averageism still probably implies that it’s good to fill the world with happy people.

First of all, most sentient beings throughout history have lived highly non-optimal lives. This is probably especially true in the multiverse. So flooding the cosmos with happy people can bump up the average.

Second, to avoid the result that it would be great if everyone who was slightly more miserable than average dropped dead, averageists generally want to maximize the average welfare people experience over the course of their life. Thus, people dying more quickly and having less welfare wouldn’t be good. It may raise average welfare at any given time, but it doesn’t increase however much welfare is experienced over a lifetime.

Similarly, we wouldn’t want to say that surviving a hemispherectomy is only good if your welfare is above average. Thus, we ought to say that what matters to the averageist is welfare across R-related streams, rather than average welfare across a lifetime. If what matters is the R-relation, then we should maximize average welfare across those who are R-related, instead of across individual lives. But then having more R-related successors is very good because it boosts welfare per R-related stream. Similar points apply to variable value theories, and these theories are also rejected by basically everyone.

4 What about non-population ethical views?

Okay, maybe there’s no way to get out of the result that it’s good to create happy people by adopting a view of population ethics. Do other philosophical views help? I can think of two that might appear to be of some service here.

First, you might think that utility is bounded. On such a view, as you add more and more good stuff to the world, the value of extra good stuff asymptotically approaches zero. One happy person added is good, the next one added is not as good, the one after that isn’t as good either. As the number of people approaches infinity, the value approaches some finite bound.

Now, bounded views might not imply that filling the universe is super good if we’ve already capped out on value. But once we’ve capped out on value, they imply it doesn’t matter what we do at all. So might as well fill it with happy people in the off-chance that they’re wrong (as they very likely are). A view on which nothing matters beyond a threshold doesn’t give one any preferential reason to disfavor one course of action beyond the threshold.

Second, you could be a negative utilitarian. You might think that preventing extreme suffering matters categorically more than creating extreme welfare. On this view, what really matters is preventing extreme suffering. Creating welfare is nice, but it matters categorically less than preventing extreme suffering.

Now, even on this view, creating happy people is still good. Negative utilitarians think suffering outweighs well-being, not that well-being isn’t good at all. And under moral uncertainty, you shouldn’t be certain of negative utilitarianism (being ecumenical, I won’t mention that negative utilitarianism is ridiculous). So then in expectation, you should still think it’s important to fill the universe with happy lives! At the very least, you should think that a world full of happy people is better than the default scenario, which may contain astronomical suffering.

5 Conclusion

It is often thought that the conclusion that it’s important to fill the universe with happy digital minds is something that only weird utilitarians have to think. Here I’ve argued it follows naturally from almost every view in philosophy. The only way out of this is by being nearly certain in negative utilitarianism or being a person-affecting view adoptee who believes in souls. Creating a bliss-filled world should be everyone’s priority, not just a utilitarian thing. This is cause for both excitement and concern. Lots of value can be brought about if we play our cards right. But by default, unless we do some very surprising thing, which we’re not on track to do, nearly all value will be lost.

item.title: Time Sensitive Urgent Animal Welfare Action
item.description: How you can prevent the federal government from destroying most animal welfare laws
item.content:encoded:
By Bentham's Bulldog

Edit: 4/29 this post has been superseded in light of recent events by this post!

The EATS act—now called the save our bacon act—would make it illegal for states to pass animal welfare laws that apply to products produced out of state. This would gut most state level animal protection. It would be the worst law for animal welfare ever passed, and would consign hundreds of millions of animals to a life in a cage. Terrifyingly, it has been added to the recent farm bill (though fortunately, even if it passes, egg laying hens will be spared). It will be voted on in the next few days, so this is EXTREMELY TIME SENSITIVE!

There is an amendment to the farm bill that representatives could vote for called the Luna amendment which would remove the EATS act from the farm bill. Edit 4/28: This amendment has been struck down, so now the remaining option is getting people to vote no on the farm bill—see the doc below for more. This would save countless animals from extreme suffering and prevent the dissolution of most animal protection laws. It would be a catastrophe for animal welfare of historic proportions.

Fortunately, there is something you can do about it. See this document for a lot more detail, including fairly easy steps like emailing your representative. Please, please, do some of these things. This is truly a pivotal moment for animals, and how we act today might affect the fates of hundreds of millions of animals. The lives of hundreds of millions of sentient beings is in flux, and whether they are kept in nightmarish cages for their whole lives comes down to what happens in the next few days.

item.title: You Cannot Vote For Demented Ghouls Who Vote To Torture Millions of Animals
item.description: And you should tell your representatives that
item.content:encoded:
By Bentham's Bulldog

(The stuff I discuss here is urgent and time sensitive, so I’d really appreciate you sharing and restacking it).

A catastrophe has reached the shores of America. But it is not a war, a bomb, or a terrorist attack. This catastrophe is distinctly moral. The current farm bill, if it passes, would be the worst legislation for animals ever passed in American history. It might very well pass. And if it does, many millions of animals will be senselessly tortured.

Various states have animal welfare laws that regulate which animal products can be sold in their state. For example, in California, you can’t sell pork or veal from animals that were kept in a cage, even if they were raised in a different state. The SOB act would eliminate these state level provisions (as applied to all but egg laying hens). It’s been snuck into the farm bill.

Most state-level animal welfare laws, therefore, would be eliminated if the farm bill passes. States would no longer be able to prevent animals kept in small crates from being sold. This would be a horrific encroachment on federalism, but that would not be its main effect.

Its main effect would be eliminating overwhelmingly popular state level laws that prevent many millions of pigs and cows from being confined in a cage. Tens of millions of animals could be affected. Not only would it destroy current state laws, it would prevent future state laws from protecting animals. It is important to be blunt here: this is an effort by pork lobbyists to make a quick buck off torturing millions of animals.

And yes, it is torture. If you kept a dog in a tiny cage where she couldn’t turn around for many months, that would uncontroversially be called torture. That is the fate that millions of pigs, who are smarter than dogs, will endure if the bill passes. Sometimes, sadists torture poor, innocent animals because they enjoy it. The congresspeople who voted for this bill, and especially who took specific efforts to keep this damned provision in the farm bill, have astronomically more animal blood on their hands than sick psychopaths who torture animals.

All across the political spectrum, bipartisan voices have sprang up opposing this craven bill. These include Tomi Lahren, Glenn Greenwald, (link), Adam Schiff, Alex Padilla, and many others. The people who supported this provision by and large did it because they are in the pockets of giant factory farms. Thinking about those spineless, gelatinous invertebrate ghouls who sold out their principles to facilitate the mass torture of the innocent, I am reminded of a line from Scott Alexander: “this goes beyond normal political lying into the sort of thing that makes you the scum of the earth, the sort of person for whom even an all-merciful God could not restrain Himself from creating Hell.”

You cannot in good conscience vote for people who support this bill. To the extent that your conscience tells you anything, it must tell you to stand up for the meek and the innocent and the vulnerable. There is no group on earth more vulnerable than farmed animals. What is at stake is their torture on an industrial scale. If conscience does not tell you not to support those who support the torture of the innocent, what could it possible tell you?

And if you cannot, in good conscience, vote for a representative who would support the farm bill in its current form, then you ought to call your representatives and tell them that. To let them know, call the House Switchboard 202-224-3121 during business hours. Tell them your zip code and they’ll connect you to your representative’s office. See this document for what to say plus for a bunch of other options for impactful things to do, including calling the congresspeople whose votes are most consequential and in flux, on behalf of the humane league. The Luna amendment, which could have removed this wicked provision from the farm bill, failed. The only remaining option is voting no on the farm bill itself.

To millions of crated pigs, this is the most important piece of legislation ever passed without any close contenders. For the animals, this is the hinge of history, and what we do in the passing days matters like little else. A generational catastrophe is at stake: please, help prevent it from becoming reality.

item.title: Book Review: All the Lives You Can Change
item.content:encoded:
By Bentham's Bulldog

Effective altruism is a social movement that’s about trying to do good as effectively as possible, with charity, career, and life projects broadly. If you go to a random local effective altruism event, most of the people there will be atheists, even in a country that’s mostly Christian. But this isn’t because of any deep conflict between Christian ideas and effective altruism. I’m in a Facebook group with a bunch of Christian philosophers, and about half of them are effective altruists in some form.

Similarly, Aron Wall who is among the most devout Christians I know, is an effective altruist and gives his money to the most effective charities he can find. My friend who runs the YouTube channel Apologetics Squared is another very religious Christian who supports effective altruism—he even made a video about how to maximally effectively spread the Gospel (hint: it’s not getting into theology arguments on the internet). Smart, philosophically-reflective Christians who take their faith seriously are effective altruists at astonishing rates.

Enter All the Lives You Can Change, released this week! It’s written by David Zhang, Dominic Roser, and J.D. Bauman. I met J.D. at an effective altruism event, and was immediately impressed by him—he seemed to radiate a kind of deep-rooted moral decency and conviction. I briefly met Dominic too at an EA for Christians event that they were generous enough to let me attend even though I’m not Christian. Incidentally, that event was where I learned from Dustin Crummett about shrimp welfare! The authors are all part of an organization called EA for Christians, about trying to promote effective altruism to Christians. This book is their attempt to popularize those core ideas.

And note, these aren’t the kinds of wishy-washy Christians whose theology stops at “Jesus was nice to people, so you should be nice too.” No, these are people who actually take Christianity seriously, who reflect seriously on what Jesus would want them to do and try hard to do it. They think effective altruism should be a core part of the Christian life. The case that they lay out for this position is very compelling.

The book was a delight to read. I finished it in two days. Like most EA books, it contained a bunch of cool stories of people doing good effectively. Like most Christian books, it included a lot of quotations of scripture. I came away more convinced that Jesus would have been supportive of effective altruism. Many of his moral claims echoed core EA claims.

Critics of EA complain that asking you to give away 10% of your wealth is too demanding, despite leaving them still richer than almost everyone who has ever lived? Oh, that’s too demanding? Try getting nailed to a cross! The whole Christian story is that morality is sufficiently demanding that none of us live up to it very well! John the Baptist says:

Whoever has two shirts should share with the person who has none, and whoever has food should do the same.

Jesus went so far as to say “If you want to be perfect, go, sell your possessions and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven. Then come, follow me.” Now, lots of Christians will interpret this passage to just be a highly specific command for that particular guy. This seems like cope. Really, the passage was included just as a specific message to that one guy which doesn’t apply more broadly? Does anyone find this kind of exegesis plausible in any other context? And don’t take it from me, here’s what Aquinas said on the matter:

Now, according to the natural order instituted by divine providence, material goods are provided for the satisfaction of human needs. Therefore the division and appropriation of property, which proceeds from human law, must not hinder the satisfaction of man's necessity from such goods. Equally, whatever a man has in superabundance is owed, of natural right, to the poor for their sustenance. So Ambrosius says, and it is also to be found in the Decretum Gratiani: "The bread which you withhold belongs to the hungry; the clothing you shut away, to the naked; and the money you bury in the earth is the redemption and freedom of the penniless."

“Do I really have to care about effectiveness?” you ask! “Yes,” Jesus answers, “you’re supposed to love your neighbor as yourself.” When deciding what to do for your own benefit, you don’t just do random things, but what benefits you most. “Okay, but surely my neighbors are just the people nearby and not people far away, so I don’t have to give to the other side of the world?” “No,” Jesus answers, and tells a long parable to show just how wrong you are:

25 On one occasion an expert in the law stood up to test Jesus. “Teacher,” he asked, “what must I do to inherit eternal life?”

26 “What is written in the Law?” he replied. “How do you read it?”

27 He answered, “‘Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength and with all your mind’[a]; and, ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’”

28 “You have answered correctly,” Jesus replied. “Do this and you will live.”

29 But he wanted to justify himself, so he asked Jesus, “And who is my neighbor?”

30 In reply Jesus said: “A man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, when he was attacked by robbers. They stripped him of his clothes, beat him and went away, leaving him half dead. 31 A priest happened to be going down the same road, and when he saw the man, he passed by on the other side. 32 So too, a Levite, when he came to the place and saw him, passed by on the other side. 33 But a Samaritan, as he traveled, came where the man was; and when he saw him, he took pity on him. 34 He went to him and bandaged his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. Then he put the man on his own donkey, brought him to an inn and took care of him. 35 The next day he took out two denarii and gave them to the innkeeper. ‘Look after him,’ he said, ‘and when I return, I will reimburse you for any extra expense you may have.’

36 “Which of these three do you think was a neighbor to the man who fell into the hands of robbers?”

37 The expert in the law replied, “The one who had mercy on him.”

Jesus told him, “Go and do likewise.”

As the authors note, this passage clearly indicates that your neighbor isn’t just the people nearby that you want to help. The Samaritans and the Israelites were mortal enemies. Your neighbor is the stranger, the foreigner, the people that your society isn’t motivated to help. The whole point of the parable is that your neighbor includes those that you’re not motivated to help.

“Okay,” you wonder, “maybe I should give away a bunch of my wealth, and care about foreigners. But do I really need to care that much about effectiveness?” In response, Jesus tells a bunch of parables that capture the importance of effectiveness. He recommends people be “shrewd as snakes and as innocent as doves.” In other words, one is supposed to be careful and smart about doing good.

In Luke 12:6–7, Jesus asks “Are not five sparrows sold for two pennies? And not one of them is forgotten before God. Why, even the hairs of your head are all numbered.” Insofar as God cares about every one of us individually, rather than seeing us as a homogenous mass, then the numbers of people we help really counts. As the authors put it:

A quote, often misattributed to Stalin, says the death of one man is a tragedy, but the death of a million is a statistic. The first part is certainly true: Every death is a tragedy. It’s also true that it can feel like a million deaths are just a statistic. But our instincts do not always capture reality; in the eyes of God, a million deaths are not a statistic, but a million tragedies.

Or, as they say elsewhere “If every person matters, then surely the prevention of a million deaths matters a million times. For the 513,434th victim, it makes all the difference in the world whether those who have the power to prevent death focus on saving many or saving just a few.”

The authors touch on most of the EA book quick hits. They make sure to mention that you can save lives for thousands of dollars and do incredible amounts of good with your career. While we often wonder what we’d have done in the past, e.g. in Nazi Germany, if we could have saved many lives, we have similar opportunities in the world today to save hundreds of lives. It is a law of nature proved beyond eight sigma that any EA book must include the following chart—this one is no exception.

The book also recounts a number of moving stories. Corrie ten Boom was a religious Christian who worked hard to save as many Jews as possible during the holocaust at great personal risk. About 800 people were saved from torture or death because of her. Had she only cared about doing some good, rather than carefully optimized for doing as much of it as possible, hundreds of extra people would have been tortured and murdered by the Nazis.

The book also covers a lot of topics that are important to Christians but that you won’t find in standard EA books. It talks about how faith can make it easier to make sacrifices for the good and discusses God’s special concern for caring for the meek and vulnerable. It analyzes interventions to maximally effectively spread the Gospel, how those compare to other interventions, and how Christians should think about animal welfare and Longtermism. It really engages, in a deep way, with how Christians specifically should be EAs, not just trying to market standard EA to Christians.

I am not a Christian, though I am an effective altruist. I came away from the book with a deeper respect for Christianity and a deeper vision of how it coheres with doing good effectively. If you are a Christian—or even if you are not—I cannot recommend it enough. If nothing else, throughout the book, I was impressed by the degree to which a lot of what Jesus said seemed to make deep sense. For a book to achieve that, and be well written, and tell you how to do good with your life, and carefully address serious and difficult questions, is a stunning success.

Most of all, in the book, and in the movement of Christians for EA, I saw the making of a beautiful thing—a kind of Christianity that, theological objections aside, is stunningly virtuous, and decent, and good. This beautiful thing has been largely non-existent for senseless, sociological reasons. It’s high time that changes. Help get and promote the book not just because it’s an awesome book full of useful information and advice, but so this beautiful thing may emerge and grow, so that the poverty and death and suffering that is within our reach can be driven out, and a version of the Gospel faithful both to its central message and what is most important in the world can emerge more fully.

item.title: "Experts Say," Um, No They Don't
item.description: A random professor's opinion isn't an expert consensus!
item.content:encoded:
By Bentham's Bulldog

One of my favorite AI hiccups that I’ve witnessed is the following:

Studies find that sexual orientation and child molestation are not the same thing? What, pray tell, did those study consist in? Did they examine sexual orientation under a microscope and find that it wasn’t the same as molesting children? What? Breaking: study in animal behavior finds that squirrels are not the same as massacre of the innocent. Breaking: study finds the integrated information theory of consciousness is not the same thing as shampoo. Did we really need studies on this?

This is a particularly comical example of a more common behavior: vaguely gesturing in the direction of experts to support a contested claim. Often this is done to defend a claim that one doesn’t really know how to defend, so they refer to some nebulous mass of experts that allegedly shares their views. This is usually very silly behavior.

For example, a while ago I read a piece discussing the comparison between transracialism and transgenderism. Now, there are obvious similarities between the two. If people feel distress with their gender, and it’s okay for them to change it, why can’t they do the same for their race? It’s a good question! Apparently, however, the experts have spoken:

Experts underscore that it is simply impossible to change your race.

“It’s just belief,” said Jamie Cohen, an assistant professor of cultural and media studies at Queens College, City University of New York. “It doesn’t ever really work, because it’s not doing anything, but they have convinced themselves that it works because there’s other people who have convinced themselves, as well.”

…

Experts agree race is not genetic. But they contend that even though race is a cultural construct, it is impossible to change your race because of the systemic inequalities inherent to being born into a certain race.

I’m sorry, what? Though race is a cultural construct, you can’t change it because there are systemic inequalities inherent to being born into a certain race? Wouldn’t the author say the same thing about gender? And why does this mean one can’t change their race? There are lots of things one can change despite being associated with inequalities—e.g. whether one is homeless. This argument seems, on its face, totally bizarre and unpersuasive.

But what’s more baffling is the deference to alleged experts. I’m sorry, experts are saying that you can’t change your race because there are systemic inequalities attached to a particular race? Which experts other than one assistant professor of cultural and media studies at Queens College have said that? And why does being a professor of cultural and media studies give one special expertise in whether it follows from the fact that some race carries with it systemic inequalities that you can’t change your race?

Here is what I suspect happened. The author was writing about transracialism, and noticed the obvious parallel with transgenderism. The standard progressive party line is that one is good and the other is bad. She thus had to concoct some explanation of the asymmetry. Unfortunately, there isn’t really any obvious asymmetry, so she said the first thing that popped in her head, declaring it to be the answer endorsed by The Experts (tm).

This is a tempting vice for writers. If there is a claim that you believe (or that is convenient for whatever you’re arguing) but you don’t have the ability to back up, it is always tempting to throw in a hyperlink, and claim “studies say [CLAIM].” But do studies really say it? Or did you just go on google scholar, google [CLAIM], find one study that sort of rhymes with it, and chuck it into the article? One study doesn’t establish anything. John Smith from Clown College in Middle-of-Nowhere Wyoming agreeing with a claim doesn’t establish that it’s supported by any kind of expert consensus.

Now, there are some claims that really are supported by experts. For example, there is very wide agreement among climate scientists that human have caused global warming. Similarly, pretty much every cosmologist thinks the universe is billions of years old, nearly every biologist believes in evolution by natural selection, and pretty much every economist thinks tariffs are bad. The last claim is only rejected by two economists, and both are Peter Navarro.1

Similarly, sometimes a study is really well done and should change your beliefs. If a study makes a powerful case for some position, it is fine to cite it and explain its implications. But the mere fact that a study says something tells us little about whether it’s true unless we know something about its methodology. You can find a study saying almost everything. In fact, a bunch of studies say homeopathy works. Beware The Man of One Study. Similarly, beware the man of one expert.

Also, there are some cases where I don’t care what the experts say. I can’t think of a single thing in the world that I care about less than the consensus that exists among professors of gender studies about, say, abortion or economics. Gender studies professors are basically all left wing, so it doesn’t tell you very much that they agree with some left wing position. Professors of sociology aren’t left-wing because reality has a left-wing bias—they’re left-wing because they have a left-wing bias. And I say that as someone who is politically left-wing! If the experts are systemically biased, then even if they mostly adopt some position, that doesn’t tell you much. I’m reminded of a joke by :

100% of experts agree Catholicism is the true religion. Our survey defined “expert” as person with rank Bishop or above in Catholic Church.

Expert consensus only matters if there’s reason to think that the alleged experts formed their belief in a way that was responsive to the truth. In many cases, there isn’t, and in many cases, the alleged experts are just horribly confused. I have somewhat left wing views on philosophy of gender (I think, for example, that one can change their gender), but I have never heard a professor of gender studies talk about the subject and be anything other than horribly confused (sadly, a common malady afflicting non-philosophers). Does anyone think that gender studies professors spend much time carefully considering the best arguments against their position, from people like Tomas Bogardus?

Now, there are some edge cases along these lines. How much, for example, should a Christian trust the consensus of biblical scholars? On the one hand, Biblical scholars often display profound philosophical confusion, and unquestioningly parrot naturalistic philosophical assumptions. On the other, they know a lot about the Bible and have spent decades of their life thinking about it. I’ve generally found the views of the Biblical scholars to make a lot of sense when I’ve looked into them—e.g. about the anonymity of the Gospels, the documentary hypothesis, and the book of Daniel—but I can see reasonable minds differing on this subject.

Similarly, I don’t take the view that a warming climate eliminated the megafauna all that seriously, even though a lot of experts believe it, because I’ve looked into the dispute, and the case against it is so overwhelming. Plus, we have a plausible error theory of why experts would falsely believe it: they succumb to the rather serious vice of not being Bayesians, and so they ignore most of the powerful circumstantial evidence. Additionally, it’s a bit unfashionable to blame things on indigenous people, so they’re somewhat biased—especially when the other potential culprit is the far more fashionable climate change.

Notably, a lot of experts in the field think the case for hunting having wiped out the megafauna is completely decisive, and are a bit embarrassed that the rest of their field hasn’t caught on. So my position is pretty mainstream. But even here where the case seems so overwhelmingly lopsided, I hold out some reasonable uncertainty on the possibility that I’m just horrendously confused about the whole dispute.

One useful heuristic along these lines is: if you notice the experts who are biased not to believe some position still end up believing it, that’s strong evidence that it’s right. It’s not definitive evidence—maybe they’re just wrong. But if the case for some position is strong enough that it convinces even those who are biased against it, that tells you something. It is notable, for example, that lots of young Earth creationists start studying biology, hoping to debunk evolution, only to start believing it after carefully examining the evidence.

So figuring out when to trust experts is a pretty subtle thing and it’s hard to get right. It’s important to avoid the twin errors of “agreeing with everything that two thirds of sociologists think about politics,” and “ignoring the overwhelming scientific consensus in favor of evolution.” But in many cases, this is done sloppily and lazily—a conversational deus ex machina said in the absence of convincing reasons to adopt one’s position. And certainly the fact that one supposed expert agrees with you is almost never any reason to think you are correct.

Serious empirical investigation can provide strong evidence for surprising claims. But if you don’t do that empirical investigation, while making claims about what that empirical investigation turned up, you’re behaving dishonestly. You are claiming to know what the experts and studies say and think when you do not. Trust the empirical literature, and the consensus of serious experts, but don’t trust every old claim anyone says the experts believe. Odds are decent that they’re just bullshitting you, especially if they are a YouTuber, Twitch streamer, or worst of all, a blogger.

1

Joke not original to me, but I forget where it’s from—maybe Jeff Maurer.
